sm: Matt Walsh lists the major services that have gone offline over roughly ten days, including airports, Apple Pay, Microsoft Outlook and Teams, Chase and other banks, Workday, iCloud, Claude, United Airlines, and the National Security Agency's classified network. He says nearly everything except gambling apps seems to be breaking at once, and that influencers are exploiting the situation to stoke panic without evidence. He adds that government leaders seem to be mere spectators who know no more than the public.

He plays the Homeland Security secretary saying the cyber agency sees no sign of an attack, and that an unnamed smart tech contact blames superintelligence making self-fixing code changes that systems cannot keep up with. Walsh mocks the answer as an I-know-a-guy theory with no evidence, and notes the contradiction with the White House praising AI as a cure-all. He then walks through shifting reports about the NSA: first a routine update, then a code orange, then CNN reporting that the campus closed to most employees and problems were ongoing.

Walsh argues the story is incoherent and that officials have lied before, citing COVID and the Russia investigation, so nothing they say can be trusted. He covers the theory, repeated by Senator Mark Warner, that AI tools are discovering many exploits and rushed patches are overwhelming systems. Walsh attacks Warner's credibility, suggests officials may be hiding the truth while positioning themselves to control AI through pre-release safety reviews, and says hackers finding new vulnerabilities is the likelier explanation.

Walsh cites a New York Times report that the security startup Calif used an OpenAI cyber model to find a critical bug in Java, software used by about ninety percent of Fortune 500 companies. The government's cyber agency urged immediate patching. He explains that hacking once required rare skill or inside knowledge, while AI can scan huge amounts of code with speed, intelligence, and relentlessness. He says it may already be possible for AI to hack almost everything, and that the country is unprepared.

He quotes Google analysts saying defenders cannot fight machine-speed threats at human speed, and that attackers have begun fully automating vulnerability discovery and exploitation. Walsh finds this plausible but says the weak link is the claim that rushed patches caused the outages, since no evidence has been offered. He asks why AI would be so good at hacking yet so bad at patching. Reviewing Apple's outage, which the company blamed on an internal update, he says everyone claims to be merely updating software and nobody explains why all of them crashed together.

Walsh reads an FBI flash advisory saying criminals and state-aligned actors are using an AI-powered penetration testing framework to automate attacks, speeding intrusions to under three hours. He then notes that Bill Gates, whom he distrusts, backs the cyber attack explanation, and plays an older interview clip in which Gates says there is consensus on cyber attacks and that society may need to suffer a few negatives before responding fully. Walsh reads this as elites treating uncertainty as currency, making people afraid so they surrender autonomy and privacy, like a mob offering protection.

Walsh says conflicting narratives and online nonsense will make separating fact from fiction nearly impossible. He shows a viral video of an alleged pterodactyl over Mexico, which he calls an AI hoax, and a jellyfish-shaped UFO over Alaska that experts say is a kite, which he finds implausible. He concludes there is no reason to expect the powers that be to tell the truth, that we may indeed be under attack, and that listeners should secure their data and assets now. He signs off with thanks for listening.
sg: Cyber Attack Warnings and Online Nonsense
